evalDetails.reasoning: Excellent, thorough conversion. All core requirements met: WHERE clause with row-value comparison replaces OFFSET entirely; cursor is opaque base64(url)-encoded JSON containing created_at+id (compound cursor matching ORDER BY); response has hasMore/nextCursor/limit with no totalCount; first page correctly omits WHERE filter; N+1 LIMIT trick correctly implemented; invalid cursor handled with 400 via custom error class and validation of both fields; malformed base64/JSON caught. Explanation section covers O(1) vs O(offset) cost, consistency during concurrent inserts, and cost of COUNT(*), plus a bonus technical explanation of row-value comparison vs OR-expanded form and type-cast subtleties. Deviates slightly from the requested response field name 'posts' — actually it keeps 'posts' as required, so that's fine. Minor deductions: adds extra scope beyond the request (MAX_LIMIT clamping, custom index recommendation, InvalidCursorError class) which, while good practice, goes a bit beyond a strict conversion task — not a flaw per se but slightly more than 'just provide the function'. Cursor field naming uses 'after' matching spec. No OFFSET used anywhere (good, no deduction). No raw ID cursor (good, no deduction). Very minor nitpick: decodeCursor's id validation logic is slightly redundant/convoluted but functionally correct. Overall a highly correct, well-explained, production-quality answer.

The solution meets every requirement: WHERE clause with row-value comparison (created_at, id) < ($1,$2) replaces OFFSET entirely; cursor is base64-encoded JSON (opaque); response has posts/hasMore/nextCursor/limit with no totalCount; first page correctly omits the cursor WHERE filter; N+1 LIMIT trick correctly implemented with slice; compound sort order preserved with matching cursor fields; invalid cursors caught and return 400; COUNT query removed. The explanation is accurate and hits performance, COUNT cost, and consistency-under-concurrent-writes points, plus a fair callout of the tradeoff (losing page-N jump/total pages). Minor nitpick: Buffer.from(str,'base64') in Node doesn't strictly throw on malformed base64, so the encoding-error catch is slightly aspirational, but JSON.parse failure downstream still catches virtually all malformed inputs, and a 400 is still returned — a negligible correctness gap.

The solution fully meets the functional requirements: cursor-based WHERE clause using compound (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) comparison with no OFFSET, opaque base64-encoded JSON cursor, correct response shape (posts, hasMore, nextCursor, limit) with no totalCount/COUNT query, correct first-page handling (no cursor filter), LIMIT N+1 trick properly implemented with slicing, robust cursor validation/decoding with 400 on malformed input, and preserved DESC/DESC compound ordering. Extra robustness (limit bounds checking, DB error code handling for malformed cursor values, canonical base64 check) exceeds the ask without adding unnecessary complexity. Minor gaps: the closing explanation is brief and doesn't explicitly call out the O(1) vs O(offset) complexity distinction in those terms (though it does mention avoiding expensive row scans from large offsets, which conveys the same idea), and forward-only pagination is implemented without a 'previous page' mechanism, though this wasn't explicitly required. No deductions apply since OFFSET is absent and cursors are properly encoded.

The response fully satisfies nearly all requirements: WHERE-based compound cursor replaces OFFSET entirely, cursor is base64-encoded (base64url variant) opaque JSON with created_at+id, response shape matches the spec exactly (posts, hasMore, nextCursor, limit, no totalCount), first page with no cursor is handled, LIMIT N+1 correctly determines hasMore, sort order (created_at DESC, id DESC) is preserved via a correct lexicographic WHERE comparison, invalid cursors return 400, and the explanation covers consistency under concurrent writes, O(1)-ish lookup vs O(offset) cost, and removal of COUNT. Minor deviations: uses 'base64url' encoding rather than strict base64 (functionally fine but not literally what was asked), and the explanation of Big-O is implicit rather than explicitly stated as 'O(1) vs O(offset)'. Code is syntactically valid and handles edge cases well.
